newsitem.title: CANADA: Hollinger says Southam bid will succeed.
newsitem.headline: Hollinger says Southam bid will succeed.

text.p: Hollinger Inc said on Thursday it would not increase its offer for the minority shares of Southam Inc, despite plans by some shareholders to reject the bid when it is put to a vote on Monday.
Hollinger Vice-President of Finance Jack Boultbee said Hollinger did not need to sweeten its offer for the shares of Southam it did not already own because the bid would succeed.
"I don't accept that (the bid will fail) by any stretch of the imagination. We'll see on Monday, won't we?" he said.
The bid, revised last week by Hollinger, is valued between C$23.55 and C$23.95 a share.

Shareholders will vote on the offer on Monday. The bid will fail if it is rejected by at least 33.33 percent of minority shareholders. Hollinger already owns 50.45 percent of the newspaper chain, Canada's largest by circulation.
Boultbee said minority shareholders were threatening not to tender their shares in order to increase Hollinger's bid, which has been adjusted once from the original offer.
"Nobody has actually rejected it. All they are trying to do is negotiate through the press, which we're not going to do," Boultbee told Reuters in a telephone interview.

Franklin Mutual Advisers Inc, a unit of Franklin Resources Inc, said on Wednesday it would not tender the 7.8 million Southam shares it controls to Hollinger's bid, joining a host of other minority shareholders who have said they opposed the deal.
"The turnaround at Southam is just beginning and we are comfortable being long-term shareholders in the company," New Franklin said.
Hollinger's original offer involved C$13.50 in cash and a C$10 non-voting special share in Hollinger Canadian, a unit of Hollinger International Inc.
Hollinger adjusted the bid last week after complaints the special shares were not worth C$10.
The board approved the deal after Hollinger changed the C$10 special share into a US$10 share with conversion privileges that kick in after six months.
Boultbee said the revised offer was a good value.
"The offer is fair. If they don't accept it, you can already see the share price is declining rapidly, so if people want to give up value they give up value. It's up to them," he said.
Southam shares were up 0.20 to 21.95 on Thursday after losing 0.50 on Wednesday.
((Andrea Hopkins at Reuters Toronto Bureau (416) 941-8102 or e-mail andrea.hopkins@reuters.com))
